p: Low-code and no-code platforms let people build apps by assembling pre-made blocks on a visual canvas, with little or no programming. They have improved a lot and, combined with AI features, are increasingly capable. Custom software, by contrast, is written specifically for your needs. Neither is universally better. The right choice depends on what you are building and how long you expect to use it.

list: Internal tools: approval forms, simple trackers, dashboards and small workflow apps for your own team.
Speed to test: you can validate an idea in days rather than months.
Lower upfront cost: you avoid paying for a full development team for a simple need.
Business-user ownership: staff who know the process can adjust it without waiting for a developer.
Complex logic: unusual rules, heavy calculations or intricate permissions can be awkward or impossible.
Integrations: connecting deeply with an ERP, CRM or third-party API often runs into platform limits.
Performance and scale: platforms can slow down or become expensive as users and data grow.
Lock-in: your app lives on the vendor's platform, and moving away may mean rebuilding it.
Recurring fees: per-user or per-app pricing can overtake the cost of custom development over several years.
Customer-facing polish: unique branding and experiences are harder to achieve.

p: Custom development makes sense when the software is core to how you compete, when you need unusual workflows, when you must integrate with several systems, when security or compliance requirements are strict, or when you expect a large number of users. You own the code, can host it where you choose, and can change anything. The trade-off is a higher initial investment and the need for ongoing maintenance.

list: Internal, low-risk, few users, simple process: try low-code.
Customer-facing product or your main revenue system: lean custom.
Needs heavy integration or unusual rules: lean custom.
Unsure of requirements: prototype in low-code, learn, then decide what to build properly.

p: Many businesses use both. A low-code tool handles quick internal workflows, while custom software powers the core product, and APIs connect the two. This keeps simple things cheap and reserves engineering effort for where it matters.

list: What happens to my data and app if the vendor raises prices or shuts down?
Can I export everything in a usable format?
What will this cost per year at three times my current users?
Does it connect to the tools I already use?
Low-code is excellent for simple internal tools and fast prototypes.
Custom software is better for core, complex or high-scale systems.
Compare the multi-year cost and the lock-in risk, not just the first month.

h: A worked example: from spreadsheet to app
p: A repair business tracks jobs in a shared spreadsheet. Technicians update status, the office calls customers, and parts are ordered from a separate list. It works until the volume grows and rows start being overwritten.

The owner first tries a low-code platform. In a couple of weeks a simple job-tracking app is running, with a form for new jobs, a status board and automatic email updates to customers. It costs little and solves the immediate problem. This is low-code at its best.

A year later the business wants parts inventory linked to supplier prices, invoices posted to its accounting system, and a customer portal under its own brand. The platform handles some of this awkwardly and charges more as users are added. At that point the owner has a clear, tested picture of what the business needs, which makes scoping a custom system far easier and less risky. The low-code app was not wasted; it served as a working specification.

list: Judging on the first month only: comparing the setup price and ignoring per-user fees over several years.
Ignoring exit options: not checking whether you can export your data and logic if you leave.
Forcing a platform to do too much: bending a simple tool to run a complex core process.
Building without an owner: letting each team create its own apps with no one responsible for security or upkeep.
Skipping a prototype: committing to custom development before testing the process in a cheaper way.
Underestimating integration: assuming connections to your other tools will be easy.
Write down the process in plain steps and mark where it is unusual.
Count how many people will use it now and in two years.
List the systems it must connect to and confirm the platform supports them.
Check data sensitivity and any compliance obligations.
Estimate the three-year cost of each option, including licences and maintenance.
Confirm you can export your data in a usable form.
Choose a small pilot to test the leading option before committing.

p: Is low-code secure? Reputable platforms invest heavily in security, but you remain responsible for how you configure access, permissions and data. Review settings and limit who can build and share apps.
Can I move from low-code to custom later? Yes, and many businesses do. Keep documentation and export your data so the move is smooth, and treat the low-code version as a prototype of requirements.
Do I need a developer for low-code? Simple apps can be built by business users. Complex logic and integrations usually benefit from developer involvement.
Which is cheaper? Low-code is usually cheaper at the start for simple needs. Custom software can be cheaper over time for complex, high-usage systems, because there are no per-user platform fees.
